entries.note: A food word from French that was originally the name of a spiced goose stew.
From French, meaning 'rotten pot', and originally the name of a stew.
From a French word meaning to make merry and eat a lot; it was also the name of a hash.
The French word for nice, borrowed four times into English as [[gave:gentle]], [[gave:genteel]], [[gave:gentile]] and [[gave:jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]].
Rob's favourite of the four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]], and the most whimsical of them.
One of the nouns that [[see:William Shakespeare]] turned into verbs.
A verb that sounds modern, but [[see:William Shakespeare]] is its first recorded written user.
An acronym for the unwritten order of English adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
From Greek [[from:meteoron]], something high in the air; in the 15th century it meant any visible atmospheric condition, which is why weather study is [[gave:meteorology]].
In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], wind and tornadoes.
In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], rain, snow and hail.
In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], auroras and rainbows.
In the 15th-century sense of [[see:meteor]], lightning and shooting stars.
The study of weather, named after the old broad sense of [[from:meteor]] even though it does not obviously involve meteors.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
One of many British regional words for types of rain.
A Scottish word for a type of rain, which Rob thinks generally means gross.
Literally a thing that is running, from Latin [[from:currentia]], running; related to [[same-root:current]].
Something running, like the current of a river; from the same Latin root as [[same-root:currency]].
From German [[from:Kupfernickel]], copper goblin, named by miners for copper-coloured ore that yields no copper; nickel has long been a nickname for the devil.
The 'devil's fart bread', containing the devil nickname [[same-root:nickel]]; Rob teases Jess for mentioning it at every opportunity.
In English from the 1500s for a ship's steersman, from a medieval Greek word for rudder sharing the root of 'ped' foot words, probably because rudders look like feet.
A borrowing of French aile, wing, so a plane has wings inside; its silent S was added to match [[see:isle]].
Its silent S was itself only added to match [[see:island]], and [[see:aisle]] then copied it.
The word whose silent S was copied by [[see:isle]].

entries.term: A Dictionary of the English Language
entries.note: [[see:Samuel Johnson]]'s famous 1755 dictionary, the first great modern-style dictionary, full of editorialised definitions and sample sentences.
[[see:Samuel Johnson]]'s dictionary defined a politician as a man of artifice, one of deep contrivance.
[[see:Samuel Johnson]] illustrated it with the sample sentence 'to make dictionaries is dull work'.
A dictionary writer, which [[see:Samuel Johnson]] famously defined as a harmless drudge.
Originally a trademarked small medicine tablet, then applied to compressed news and papers smaller than [[see:broadsheet]]s; only later linked with sensationalism.
A massive newspaper format; Rob says few true broadsheets remain because most British papers switched to the smaller [[see:Berliner]].
A much smaller newspaper format that most [[see:broadsheet]]s have switched to.
Overly detailed synonyms journalists use to avoid repetition, named after such a phrase used for a crocodile.
A [[see:knobbly monsters]] phrase journalists used to avoid repeating the word badger.
A [[see:knobbly monsters]] phrase used for [[see:Darth Vader]].
Named by [[see:Erik the Red]] to attract settlers even though it is not green, the opposite tactic to [[see:Iceland]].
Named by [[see:Flóki Vilgerðarson]] to scare people off, because it was a terrible place to settle.
From St Lawrence Iroquoian [[from:kanata]], village; [[see:Jacques Cartier]] used it for one area, and a false story derives it from Spanish or Portuguese 'nothing here'.
Subject of a myth that it came from a misunderstood phrase meaning 'I don't know', given as the answer to 'what is that animal?'
The 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, which, despite the name, are not the ones that became birds; they include [[see:Stegosaurus]].
The 'lizard-hipped' dinosaurs, which are the ones that became birds, unlike the [[see:ornithischians]].
Named in 1877 by [[see:Othniel Charles Marsh]] from Greek [[from:stegos]], roof, and [[from:sauros]], lizard, because he thought its plates lay flat like shingles.
Its -dom is Old English for a law or judgment, not related to [[unrelated:dominion]] but to [[same-root:doom]], so it is a territory defined by decree.
Looks as if it shares the -dom of [[unrelated:kingdom]], but it doesn't.
From Old English dom, a law or judgment, later a decision determining fate; it shares that root with [[same-root:kingdom]].
An old word for judges, related to [[same-root:doom]].
[[see:William the Conqueror]]'s big volume recording who owned what land, mentioned alongside [[see:doom]].
Originally referred to the ruler's palace rather than the office; the Egyptian word means great house.
Originally described a well-fed horse, energetic and more likely to win a race, not people eating beans.
Only compared since the late 19th or early 20th century; before that people compared [[see:apples to oysters]].
The earlier comparison, recorded from the 1670s in phrases like 'as like an apple to an oyster', before [[see:apples and oranges]].
Contains [[from:deer]]: a 'wild-deer-ness' is a place full of wild beasts.
In Old English it meant any wild quadruped, not only a deer; it is hidden inside [[gave:wilderness]].
From Latin [[from:contra]], against, meaning the land lying in front of you; it has nothing to do with borders.
Thought to come from French [[from:poupée]], doll, which also gave [[same-root:puppet]] and [[same-root:poppet]].
From the same French word for doll as [[same-root:puppy]].
From the same French word for doll as [[same-root:puppy]].
Classic dog name from Latin [[from:fidus]], faithful, related to [[same-root:fidelity]]; a famous 1940s Italian Fido waited daily for his dead owner and has a statue.
Related to the dog name [[same-root:Fido]].
First recorded with this spelling in [[see:The Merchant of Venice]]; [[see:William Shakespeare]] modelled it on a similar Hebrew name of a minor biblical figure.
Usually a surname until [[see:William Shakespeare]] used it as a first name in [[see:The Tempest]].
Possibly from a Welsh name, or French-inspired; it wasn't popular until [[see:King Lear]].
Sometimes credited to [[see:William Shakespeare]], although it was already a popular name on the Continent.
The same name as [[same-root:Seamus]], taken from the [[see:vocative case]] used to address a Seamus; both are forms of [[same-root:James]].
The name behind [[gave:Hamish]], which is Seamus in the vocative case; a form of [[same-root:James]].
The grammatical form used to address someone directly; an overheard vocative of [[see:Seamus]] gave [[see:Hamish]].
The name behind both [[same-root:Hamish]] and [[same-root:Seamus]], and itself the same as [[same-root:Jacob]].
The same name as [[same-root:James]].
A word lent to another language and then borrowed back, like [[see:tennis]] and [[see:artichoke]].
A [[see:boomerang word]] from French [[from:tenez]], 'take', called out when hitting the ball; French borrowed tennis back for the sport and for tennis shoes.
So called because commoners played it on foot, not on horseback like 1700s gentlemen's sports, not because the ball is kicked.
A yearly game in rural Derbyshire played on foot with little kicking, explained by the original sense of [[see:football]].
A British English term, short for [[from:association football]].
A Caribbean island nation, the only country named after a real historical woman: [[from:Saint Lucy of Syracuse]], because French sailors arrived on her feast day.
[[see:Joseph Heller]]'s novel was originally called Catch-18 but renamed because [[see:Mila 18]] was coming out at the same time.
A book with 18 in its title coming out at the same time, which caused [[see:Catch-22]] to be renamed.
English is the only Germanic language to keep this word, originally 'scratch' and linked to runes; the others use words related to [[see:scribe]].
A Latin-derived word whose relatives other Germanic languages use for writing; it also originally meant something like scratch, as did [[see:write]].
A school of fish is borrowed from Middle Dutch and related to [[same-root:shoal]], but unrelated to the educational [[unrelated:school]].
Related to [[same-root:school]] in the sense of a group of fish.
The educational school is a Latin and Greek word whose basic sense is leisure; its spelling converged with the fish [[unrelated:school]].
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of the nautical words English got from Dutch.

entries.term: A Caveat or Warning for Common Cursitors, Vulgarly Called Vagabonds
entries.note: A mid-1500s work of [[see:Tudor rogue literature]] by [[see:Thomas Harman]] that sorted vagrants and criminals into categories such as [[see:rufflers]].
Entertainment about the people the Tudor elites considered trashy.
Former soldiers who harassed people, a category in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s book.
Horse thieves, a category in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s book.
People who faked seizures and medical emergencies to rob people, a category in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s book.

entries.term: Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue
entries.note: [[see:Francis Grose]]'s 18th-century dictionary of slang collected around London, its docks and universities; it's unclear how much he invented.

entries.term: hoddy doddy, all arse and no body
entries.note: According to [[see:Francis Grose]], 18th-century London slang for a clumsy person.
From Air Force slang, picturing a loop-the-loop going wrong; the formal word for pear-shaped is [[see:pyriform]].
The word for something that is pear-shaped.
Middle English, originally spelled loupe: a narrow vertical slit in a fortification for archers and musketeers, unrelated to other kinds of [[unrelated:loop]].
Probably coined in 1995 by Puerto Rican comedian and DJ [[see:Silverio Pérez]] as [[from:chupacabras]], 'goats sucker'; English misread the final S as a plural.
Latin for 'I will please', from the opening of a prayer and later applied to drugs; its opposite is [[see:nocebo]].
The opposite of a [[see:placebo]], Latin for 'I will cause harm'; it sounds made up but is legitimate.
A Germanic word thought to mean dry, probably from a seafaring phrase for dry goods or barrels, later narrowed to what apothecaries sold.
A rebracketing of [[from:cybernetics]]: the N belongs to Greek [[from:kybernetes]], steersman, so it should really be 'cybern'.
The first spam came when [[see:Richard Depew]] accidentally posted one message 200 times to Usenet in 1993; a user called it spam after the [[see:Spam sketch]].
The Monty Python sketch with Vikings singing 'spam', which gave its name to [[gave:spam]].
Feels like science fiction, but the word is centuries old.
One of Britain's current intelligence agencies, alongside [[see:MI6]] and GCHQ.
James Bond's service, one of Britain's current intelligence agencies alongside [[see:MI5]].
One of the British military intelligence sections, which went up to [[see:MI9]] at the end of the First World War.
One of the British military intelligence sections at the end of the First World War.
One of the British military intelligence sections at the end of the First World War.
One of the British military intelligence sections at the end of the First World War.
One of the British military intelligence sections at the end of the First World War.
One of the British military intelligence sections at the end of the First World War.
The highest-numbered British military intelligence section at the end of the First World War.
Before the 1930s just a machine operator; the [[see:Pinkerton Detective Agency]], unpopular after violent strike-breaking, called its agents operatives instead of detectives.
Became unpopular as violent strike-breakers, so it renamed its detectives [[see:operative]]s.
A French rendering of Miami-Illinois [[from:shikaakwa]], pungent wild garlic or leeks; the word also meant skunk, and its root may mean to urinate.
Means fort at the breast-shaped hill: [[from:chester]] is fort, and man- shares an ancient root with [[same-root:mammal]].
A place-name element meaning fort, like [[same-root:caster]] and [[same-root:cester]].
A place-name element meaning fort, like [[same-root:chester]].
A place-name element meaning fort, as in [[see:Leicester]].
An example of the fort element [[see:cester]].
Shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root:Manchester]].
Maybe shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root?:Manchester]].
Shares an ancient root with the man- in [[same-root:Manchester]].
The company fought generic use of its name for photocopiers, with slogans like 'when you use Xerox the way you use aspirin, we get a headache'.
From an Italian word for a bobbin used in spinning, one of several spacecraft words from textile arts, like [[see:shuttle]].
Long a word for a dart or missile, but the shuttling vehicle and space shuttle come from the weaving shuttle moving back and forth.
A word that could theoretically exist but doesn't, as with a 'groomal' to match [[see:bridal]], or [[see:liver]] for a living person.
Originally the compound bride-ale, a party with ale for a bride, which is why there is no 'groomal'; compare [[see:scythe ale]].
A Middle English harvest party, another ale party word like the bride-ale behind [[see:bridal]].
Can't be used for someone who is alive because it would clash with the organ, leaving a [[see:lexical gap]].
Jess's proposed word for the [[see:lexical gap]] of someone who has had sex, but not much.
A historical term for sex, recorded centuries ago.
A historical term for sex, recorded centuries ago.

entries.term: being at the service of Venus
entries.note: A historical term for sex, recorded centuries ago.
From Greek [[from:stoa]], porch, because its founder [[see:Zeno]] lectured on a decorated porch at the agora in Athens.
From Greek [[from:kynikos]], doglike, perhaps for the coarse lifestyle of [[see:Antisthenes]]'s followers, or perhaps after [[from?:Kynosarges]], where he taught.
The gymnasium near Athens where [[see:Antisthenes]] taught, its name meaning grey dog; possibly where [[gave?:cynic]] comes from.
Started in 1893 by [[see:Caleb Bradham]] as Brad's Drink, renamed Pepsi-Cola in 1898 because it was advertised to relieve [[from:dyspepsia]].
Originally called BackRub because the system checked backlinks to estimate a site's importance.
Meaningless Danish-looking gibberish chosen in 1959 in the Bronx by [[see:Reuben Mattus]] and [[see:Rose Mattus]] to sound foreign.
A variant of the same word as [[same-root:curse]], having lost its R, like [[see:ass]] and [[see:bust]].
The same word as [[same-root:cuss]].
A variant of [[same-root:arse]] that lost its R, like [[see:cuss]].
The R-ful form of [[same-root:ass]].
A variant of [[same-root:burst]] that lost its R, like [[see:cuss]].
The R-ful form of [[same-root:bust]].
A name for losing a sound in some versions of a word, as in [[see:cuss]] from [[see:curse]].
A starter in British English and other languages but the main dish in North America, after wartime and Depression-era restaurants made it filling enough to replace the roast.
The Dutch city's name means the hedge; Den Haag is short for [[from:'s-Gravenhage]].
The full Dutch name behind [[gave:The Hague]], referring to the hedge around the count's hunting grounds.
From Arabic [[from:al-Qahira]], the victorious, given by the conquering Fatimid caliph; medieval writers linked it to an Arabic name for Mars rising at the conquest.
In the late 16th century, a horse race where riders followed a leader's erratic course in a staggered pattern like flying wild geese; no geese involved.
Its first member may be [[see:Lord Cholmondeley]], who bet in 1785 he could have sex in a hot-air balloon; the term predates planes flying a mile high.
An English aristocrat, pronounced 'Chumley', who bet [[see:Lord Derby]] he could have sex in a hot-air balloon, possibly founding the [[see:Mile High Club]].
Tiramisu is a sentence, regional Italian for 'pick me up', perhaps for its coffee or, by speculation, invented at a brothel as an aphrodisiac.
Invented in 1943 near Texas by maître d' [[from:Ignacio Anaya]], nicknamed Nacho, for US officers' wives; he named them nachos especiales.
From Latin [[from:delirare]], to go off the furrow ([[from:lira]]), the classical equivalent of [[equivalent:off the rails]]; related to [[same-root:delirium]].
Like [[same-root:delirious]], from Latin for going off the furrow.
The modern equivalent of the furrow image in [[equivalent:delirious]].
A Latin term [[see:Sigmund Freud]] never used; he wrote in German and said [[equivalent:Es]], 'the it'.
A Latin term [[see:Sigmund Freud]] never used; he wrote in German and said [[equivalent:Ich]], 'the I'.
A Latin term [[see:Sigmund Freud]] never used; he wrote in German and said [[equivalent:Über-Ich]], 'the over-I'.
[[see:Sigmund Freud]]'s own German term, rendered in English as [[equivalent:id]].
[[see:Sigmund Freud]]'s own German term, rendered in English as [[equivalent:ego]].
[[see:Sigmund Freud]]'s own German term, rendered in English as [[equivalent:superego]].
From Arabic [[from:al-zahr]], the die, via French; first a dice game, then a risk, and the pronounced H is an overcorrection.
From Arabic via Italian and Spanish, once spelled many ways; a [[see:boomerang word]] borrowed back into Levantine Arabic as [[gave:ardi shawki]].
Levantine Arabic borrowing of English [[from:artichoke]], reshaped by folk etymology.
Not an artichoke; its 'Jerusalem' is Italian [[from:girasole]], sunflower.
From [[from:Zanni]], the servant clown of commedia dell'arte; a noun before it was an adjective.
A recurring commedia dell'arte servant clown, a Venetian form of [[from:Gianni]], pet form of [[from:Giovanni]]; it gave [[gave:zany]].
From French for 'to stuff', because farces were comic relief stuffed into serious productions to pad them out, such as during set changes.
Descends from the same ancient forked letter as [[same-root:U]], [[same-root:V]], [[same-root:W]] and [[same-root:Y]], with the fork leaned over.
Originally the same letter as [[same-root:V]], from the ancient forked letter.
The ancient forked letter with its stalk shortened; originally the same letter as [[same-root:U]].
Just a doubled [[from:U]] or [[from:V]].
Closest in shape to the ancient forked letter; it represents the Greek use of it and is called a 'Greek I' in some languages.
Minuscules came from [[from:Roman cursive]], which simplified the majuscules over the Roman Empire to make writing quicker.
Everyday Roman handwriting that developed as literacy spread and gave [[gave:lowercase letters]].
From Spanish [[from:mestengo]], a stray, from the [[from:Mesta]] livestock association, not because the horses are mixed breed.
The Honourable Council of the Mesta, a livestock owners' association whose name is said to mean mixed, maybe for dividing mixed strays; behind [[gave:mustang]].
From Spanish, meaning someone who is affectionate, directly related to [[same-root:affectionate]]; rather than an expert, someone fond of something.
Directly related to [[same-root:aficionado]].
The band spelled it L-E-D to stop people saying 'Leed Zeppelin'.
Its juke is from a Wolof and Gullah word for rowdy; the coin-operated machine was named after [[from:juke joint]]s.
A place in the south-eastern US where Black people danced, drank and gambled; it gave its name to the [[gave:jukebox]].
A word that looks like one in another language but means something different, like [[see:empathy]] and modern Greek [[see:empatheia]].
From Greek empatheia, passion or inner feeling; a [[see:false friend]] of modern Greek [[same-root:empatheia]].
In modern Greek it means animosity or malevolence, making it a [[see:false friend]] of English [[same-root:empathy]].
A German [[see:false friend]] meaning a vintage car.
A German [[see:false friend]] meaning a projector, not a car.
A German [[see:false friend]] meaning a backpack with one strap.
German for a mobile phone, borrowing an English word that doesn't exist in that sense, to Rob's innocent amusement.
Slang made by reversing words, the likely source of [[gave:moniker]], [[gave:yob]] and [[gave:slop]].
Most likely [[from:back slang]] of an eke-name, the source of [[same-root:nickname]]; it oddly sounds more formal than nickname.
From an eke-name, misdivided as a nickname; reversed in [[see:back slang]], it comes close to [[same-root:moniker]].
[[see:back slang]] for boy.
[[see:back slang]] for police.
Traced to [[see:Aretha Franklin]]'s 1967 'Respect' line 'give me my propers', shortened in Black slang; [[see:Otis Redding]]'s version lacked the line.
From Old French, literally 'made of hemp', so related to and practically a doublet of [[same-root:cannabis]].
Related to [[same-root:canvas]], practically a doublet.
A type of canvas whose duck is from a Dutch word for cloth; strips of it led to [[gave:duct tape]].
Named after non-adhesive strips of [[from:cotton duck]]; the name passed to plastic-coated adhesive tape used by Second World War soldiers.
Borrowed from Dutch [[from:ezel]], donkey, a static version of a load-bearing animal, so a canvas on an easel is a donkey carrying weed.
Its rules are identical but its prestige inverted: dropping Rs is prestigious in Received Pronunciation, less prestigious in New England.
From Old Norse 'at do', since Norse marked infinitives with at instead of to; it means much the same as a [[equivalent:to-do]].
A big fuss, essentially the same as [[equivalent:ado]].
The Old English version of the word that Old Norse gave as [[same-root:skirt]]; both meant a short garment, as do [[same-root:shorts]].
The Old Norse version of [[same-root:shirt]], meaning a short garment.
Also in the same family as [[same-root:shirt]] and [[same-root:skirt]], all short garments.
Uses an old sense of [[see:hoot]], a tiny amount, with nothing to do with owls.
Once meant the tiniest possible amount, the sense in [[see:couldn't give two hoots]].

entries.term: wouldn't touch someone with a ten-foot pole
entries.note: In the mid-1800s it was a 40-foot pole, alongside the [[equivalent:barge pole]] version; the Grinch needs a 39-and-a-half-foot pole.
A mid-1800s variant of the [[equivalent:wouldn't touch someone with a ten-foot pole]] saying, the pole being 8 to 16 feet.
Sleight of hand; built from Latin [[from:praestigiator]], juggler or trickster, when a 19th-century French magician, [[see:Jules de Rovère]], added the digit bit.
From French [[from:sorcier]], so Rob grumbles that it should really just be 'sorcier' without the extra syllable.
The Old English plural was fishes; using fish as its own plural is a Middle English invention.
Its cuttle means bag or pouch, probably related to [[same-root?:cod]]; it belongs to the genus [[see:sepia]].
Probably related to the cuttle in [[same-root?:cuttlefish]].
Latin for cuttlefish and the genus name of [[see:cuttlefish]]; in English it became the brown pigment once made from their ink, hence sepia photo filters.
From medieval Latin [[from:dies mali]], evil days (two per month on calendars); first 'in the dismal', so 'dismal day' is tautological.
From Latin [[from:caseus]], a very early borrowing into Germanic straight from the Romans, like [[see:wine]].
From Latin [[from:vinum]], a very early borrowing into Germanic straight from the Romans, like [[see:cheese]].
From German: a child garden not because children play in a garden, but a figurative garden where they grow like little flowers.
A German military acronym for [[from:Fliegerabwehrkanone]], anti-aircraft cannon; extended in WWII to the exploding shells, and now to any criticism.
